summary: Fixes earlier specifications that used underscored DNS node names before a registry existed. Now that RFC 8552 defines the registry, this document updates those specifications so they register and use their names correctly. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8553 updates older specifications that use underscores at the start of DNS names. It directs those names to a shared IANA registry so new uses can be coordinated.

subtitle: Align older underscored DNS names with the shared IANA registry.

tldr.problem: Specifications created underscored DNS node names without a shared registry, so separate names could be assigned from the same space without coordination.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8553 updates specifications that use underscored TXT, SRV, and URI records and adjusts templates so the global underscored name is registered in the shared registry.
tldr.outcome: The changes preserve existing naming practices while directing future specifications to the integrated registry defined by RFC 8552.

today: RFC 8553 is a Best Current Practice. It updates earlier specifications to use the shared underscored-name registry defined by RFC 8552.

sections.title: Why Underscored DNS Names Needed Coordination
sections.content:
An underscore at the start of a DNS node name creates a space for names that identify how a resource record is interpreted. Earlier specifications created these names without a common registry, so their assignments were not coordinated.

RFC 8552 created the shared registry for globally scoped underscored names. RFC 8553 updates existing specifications to acknowledge and use that registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Underscored names are used for special DNS records. A shared registry helps prevent separate specifications from claiming the same global name.

sections.title: Which Resource Records Are Covered
sections.content:
The document groups existing uses by the resource-record type they scope: TXT, SRV, and URI. For each type, the global underscored node name is the one closest to the DNS root.

The record-specific specifications still define what information appears below that name. The registry coordinates the top-level name, not every detail of each record's contents.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry tracks the top-level underscored name for each use. The specification for the resource-record type still explains how the records themselves work.

sections.title: How Specifications Register Names
sections.content:
Specifications that use TXT records are expected to register their global underscored node names. The same rule applies to SRV protocol names and to URI protocol or highest-level Enumservice names.

RFC 8553 also updates the SRV and URI templates to point to the shared registry. For DNSSEC trust-anchor signaling, the name prefix _ta- is registered as a single entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A specification that introduces an underscored global name should request an entry in the registry. The rule covers names used with TXT, SRV, and URI records.

sections.title: Changes to the SRV and URI Templates
sections.content:
The SRV template continues to use an underscored protocol name, such as _tcp or _udp, but says that the global name should be registered. The URI template similarly points to the registry for its global service-related name.

These changes make the registration expectation visible to editors of future revisions while retaining the existing name format.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing underscore labels keep their format. The updated templates make it clear that their global names belong in the shared registry.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8553 states that it raises no security issues. Its purpose is to coordinate names already used by DNS specifications, not to change how DNS records are secured or interpreted.

The document introduces no new IANA registry or registration process; it uses the registry defined by RFC 8552.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC makes registry and specification updates, not a new security mechanism. It uses the existing shared registry rather than creating another one.
